utterances.text: Is it correct that he gave you instructions as to the transport of dead Serb soldiers from the frontline? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he advised you to go to the technical school at Karakaj and Celopek and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you refer to a certain number of those dead people and you give a certain figure, I understood what you said on page 2 in your supplementary statement, that each body was in a black or white plastic bag and it was given a number, and that the number was placed in the bag together with the body and then the bodies were buried. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, the authorities and you yourself who were doing the actual work did everything you could to keep their bodily remains intact so that they could later be identified and taken over by family members, as should be done in accordance with the regulations in such cases; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 7, you speak of the transfer from Drinjaca to Gero's slaughterhouse, where the pathologists were at that time, weren't they? And then you say that you saw a pile of bodies, some of which were in uniform, others in civilian clothing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were all male, Muslims, that you saw that they had been killed with fire from automatic weapons. Since you said that you were on a moving truck on this particular occasion, which you didn't leave, how could you see from a moving truck - just explain that to me, please - to see not only that they were dead but also how they had been killed, what weapons had been used, and so on? Am I right in assuming that these are assumptions on your part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: When I arrived, they were all on a pile, all these dead bodies, so these are my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to hear. So you didn't see any of this. You didn't see what weapons were used, nor where, nor how but you are assuming that they were killed with firearms, automatic or semi-automatic or non-automatic. I assume that you weren't specific in your statement anyway.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you loaded onto the truck 15 or 20 bodies and that another 15 to 20 remained.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Maybe even more remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you transported them from the culture centre in Celopek - you have this on page 6, paragraph 1 - "The guards said that some Muslims had died there." Is that right, the guards at the gate? And were there cases of some people dying rather than being killed among the bodies that you transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: There were killed people and there were also people who had died. And there were some who went on a hunger strike and died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you could not make a distinction as to whether they had been killed. Well, of course, those who died, they died without any weapons being used. But in the case of those who -- whose death was caused by the use of firearms, you could not assume who was killed in battle or who may have been killed in some other -- under some other circumstances; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to gather, where the bodies were collected, once you saw them there, you didn't know whether they had been killed or whether they died, because they were brought there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No, no, they were killed there, on that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know, when you were not present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: That's what people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, please, on page 6, in the fifth paragraph, you say - and that is something I wish to clear up with you - when you say that that is what people said, that these were bodies of Muslims who, as you say, were shot and killed. In the Serbian variant of the language, we would say "streljan" or "executed" for those who were executed, whereas, in the Croatian variant, they say "ustreljen", for those executed. But tell me, please, do you have any knowledge when you say some people were executed, or do you use the term to mean that they were shot with firearms? I don't know whether you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you say "ustreljen", you mean killed by the use of firearms, not executed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I just wanted to clear that up, because according to the Croatian version, "ustreljen" means "streljan" and, being a Serb, I don't think that you would use that term for somebody who was not executed but was hit by a bullet from a firearm and was killed. So you don't have any knowledge as to anyone actually being executed, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: As you were talking about the way the bodies were marked in the bags, you also mention a wooden stick or a metal plate with the number carved in. Is it true that those numbers corresponded to the documents used by the pathologists who were doing the postmortems and that they were done in that way precisely for the purpose of identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your supplementary statement, on page 3, you say that in 1992 some people were transferred to the cultural centre in Pilica and that a certain number of people were killed in the cultural centre and that they were buried in Pilica. I'm not quite sure what you're referring to. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: That is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I thought it was a mistake. Because by checking out the information, I couldn't believe that you could have said such a thing. So that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: They were transferred from the cultural centre in Pilica, from Pilica to Bijeljina, and then exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional information, because I didn't even ask you that question. But I'm very glad that you provided that additional explanation, which is very important. So they were transferred from the cultural centre, driven to Bijeljina in order to be exchanged there, where they were in fact exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you this in a way, when we were talking about Zvornik, but to be quite sure, as we are now talking about the entire area and your entire testimony about what you were doing throughout that period, did I come to the proper conclusion that you were not an eyewitness of a single murder or killing, be it of an individual or a group or of any battling, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what I'm saying is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you witness a killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No, I was never a witness of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's make it quite clear. My question was: Is it right that you were not a witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please -- let me just see where I noted this down. The only shooting that you were a witness of was when you were shot at from Kula Grad, when you were collecting bodies in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is what I was able to gather from your statement and from your testimony. On page 4, paragraph 1 of your supplementary statement, will you please explain this for me; you talk about the transfer of bodies from Bijeli Potok to Crni Vrh and Konjevica Polje. You say that you saw two trucks passing through Karakaj and then you followed the trucks in your own car and they stopped next to the mass grave that had already been dug, 6 metres deep, 2 to 3 metres wide. Could you explain what this was all about? Because it's not quite clear. True enough, I didn't have enough time to look at it carefully because you were moved up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: They were transferring bodies from another grave to this one. They were digging them up and burying them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any reason for this? I asked you why this was being done. Why were bodies moved from one grave to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those bodies identified, the bodies who were buried there? Was that grave exhumed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I heard that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know whether they were identified and what happened in that connection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you hid on a hill which was about 50 metres away from the grave, from the tomb. Why were you hiding at all? Were you in any kind of danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to the conclusion that you were in danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No one should know if I went to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think -- just tell me whether my thinking is logical. I think that you assumed that someone was doing something in secret; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And because you assumed that they were doing something in secret, you felt that for your own safety it was better for that person or those persons doing something in secret not knowing that you were witnessing it. And could you establish who those people were who were doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't masked, I assume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, they weren't masked, but they were a long way away and I wasn't able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to clear up, to see whether we could arrive at some more facts about that. All right. You say you weren't able to identify the people, but were you able to establish whose trucks they were or things like that? You weren't able to do that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, there were no license plates, there was nothing written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as this was done from one to another, you don't know how those people were killed or came to have that fate and how they were transferred from one burial site to another, and you're certain that the burial site was exhumed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, the grave was exhumed. Now, how, in what way, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where is the grave located? Where is it on your map? We don't have to take out the map and lose time over that, but where was it? Just tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, Crni Vrh. Right. Very well. Now, I've made a note of something here while you were testifying. You said -- let's see, six localities, six locations, sites that I noted down. Please put me right if I'm wrong. So the village of Pilica, Sahbegovici, Crni Vrh, Glumina, Kamenica, and Drinjaca. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have I omitted some place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Jusici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Jusici, right. So Jusici, one more. Now, tell me this, please: In which period of time were you there taking over the bodies, these dead people, and taking them off to be buried, as you said mostly to the Muslim cemetery? I don't want to have to search for its name, it's not important. But what period of time was this? When were you doing this? When were you doing that job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means a full three years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, during those three years, can you roughly tell me what was the total number of bodies of those persons, Muslims, who were killed that you buried? How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, because it was a long time ago and all the rest of it. But not to exaggerate, let me say about 500 corpses. 500 corpses in the space of three years. Yes, that's right. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's your estimate on the basis of what you did, and everything passed through your hands; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: Is it true and correct that for the line, for the fighters, for the frontline, you transported 5.000 coffins for the killed Serbs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Exact. Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were those people buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Our Serbs, our fighters, were buried and so were the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these people, were they killed up at the frontline in your area where the fighting was going on? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: It is from Bijeljina to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the frontline from Bijeljina to Vlasenica? That's what you're talking about; right? And that's where you transported these 5.000 coffins.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, yes. But they went off in other directions too, not only to that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should be told that you have ten minutes left for your hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I should like to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank the witness. I think that he has provided me the answers to all the essential questions that I had to ask him, without entering into too much detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the floor. I have just one brief topic to deal with in open session, and then several other questions in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you spoke about the fact that a portion of people, especially young Muslims, at their own desire you transported and drove off towards Tuzla. Can you tell us how many there were of these young Muslims and also other people of different ages whom you drove towards Tuzla during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I transported two soldiers who had come from Serbia, and about seven elderly persons from Zvornik. There you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in something else. Towards Serbia was there -- were there Muslims leaving who wanted to escape the conflicts or who were in jeopardy? So were there Muslims fleeing to Serbia and from thence to other people [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: A large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I see, a large number. Can you give us a rough idea of how many? Did they go of their own free will? Did they go voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Many of them went to Serbia. I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were there Serbs of Serb ethnicity who were leaving Bosnia because they were afraid they would lose their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; there were Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough estimate of the number? Was it a large number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, a large number of people that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go into private session for a few moments now, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the 5.000 coffins that you mentioned in your statement on page 6 and that Mr. Milosevic has asked you about, to be clear, these coffins are coffins with bodies in them or these are empty coffins?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Empty coffins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And these coffins were designated for the frontline to be used to bury Serb soldiers or Serb and Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Serb and Muslim as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic went through a rather lengthy list of people who had been killed and described some of their brutal injuries. I just want to ask you a few detailed questions about that. Can you tell us again, what were the injuries that this Radomir Pavlovic suffered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that, but I know the details. I know that I went there, took over the body. There were all sorts of injuries. But I can't remember. It was a long time ago, a long time ago. It's not that there were just five or six or ten of them. There were a great many of them, so I can't remember on whichever side, either on one side or as to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How about Mr. Dragomir Bozic? Do you have a specific memory -- recollection today what his injuries were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I can't remember all the injuries and how each individual one was injured. But I just remember the places I went to and how I took over the bodies. Now, as to the injuries, I can't remember because they were usually in bags and wrapped up in blankets and then we would load them up and drive off. So I didn't look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So at least -- and these -- for the case of these two particular men, when Mr. Milosevic described their specific injuries, you have no independent recollection of whether or not his description of those injuries were correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, objection. The question is not one that is proper because it is one thing when I tell the witness the name of the village, the place, the date, and all the rest of it, and then I quote the name of the man in question, and it's quite another thing when Mr. Groome asks him out of the blue from all this mass of facts just a name and surname. Then of course it is impossible for the witness to remember in that way, without having the preliminary details quoted to him. So I think that the question is quite improper because it is impossible for him to know off the bat the names of the people, of course, with the injuries. But it is understandable, reasonable, logical when I quote the time, the place, the location, and the people in question, then he will remember. Mr. Groome is intentionally asking him in the way in which the witness cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness can be asked is this: These events took place ten years ago. Do you have - as he was asked - any independent recollection of these particular events or specific injuries? If he has, he can tell us. If he hasn't, then he can tell us that too. Now, Mr. Groome, would you like to rephrase your question in that way, effectively repeating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've heard His Honour's question to you. Do you have an independent recollection today about these -- these particular cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I don't remember the injuries because it wasn't my custom to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the injuries that Mr. Milosevic put to you, is it your testimony that you did not yourself look at the condition of these bodies and make those observations yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a matter that you heard that these people suffered this type of injuries? Is that how you have this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you heard about this information from what sources? From newspapers or radio or individuals? Can you please describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: On the radio and in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic put to you - I'm just quoting a passage of the record - "Yes, but the point is that the Muslims were buried at the Muslim cemetery regularly and in accordance with regular procedure applied in such cases." And I believe you said that that was true. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, a portion of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time in Zvornik that the Muslim cemetery became filled and there was no more room for additional burials, or was there always room to expand the number of graves at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: The cemeteries were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the regular procedure for a Muslim being buried - correct me if I'm wrong - is that a monument or a pillar is placed at the head of the grave and at the foot of the grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you've described to us - and I'm quoting you now from the record, in reference to Glumina - "Well, that's where 200 to 250 bodies were buried in sacks, and they were numbered and they were in two rows." The question I have for you now is: Was Glumina a Muslim cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were the bodies that were buried at Glumina, were they buried according to the procedure that you've just described, the pillar at the head and the pillar at the foot of the -- of the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you -- in response to questions put to you by the accused, you talked about a reburial. I want to ask you a few questions about that reburial. Do you know who ordered the reburial of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: From the Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You need to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: N1 and N2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know -- how do you know that those two people ordered the -- the removal or the reburial of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, N3 and N4 passed it on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's the names listed on tab 2 of Prosecution Exhibit 452, that list of names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You need to answer verbally for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you thought that the reburial of the bodies was done in secret. What was it about what you observed that made you believe that it was being done in secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, so that it wouldn't be discovered. They were transported from one to another so that it wouldn't be found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from where precisely were the bodies taken and where precisely were the bodies moved to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I don't know. Where they were taken from, I don't know. But where they were transported later on, then those from the international organisation did that, at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you describe what equipment was used to -- to rebury these bodies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: They were just thrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thrown from what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, they were dug up and unloaded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any heavy equipment used, such as bulldozers or backhoes or the like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were machines like that up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see them being used to move these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: Well, if they were there, they must have been used. That's quite usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question to you is: Are you able to approximate for us the number of bodies that you saw being removed and reburied in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you need to answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: No, I can't do that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate for us the number of trucks that were used in this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that there has been a misunderstanding. May I just ask one additional question of this witness, just one additional question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to deal with the misunderstanding because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the misunderstanding that you want clarified?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to ask the witness this: As I understand from his answers, which were affirmative, I understood that you had personally seen some bodies without a head or without arms and legs or butchered. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with it in this way: You are now being asked about, as I understand it, the mutilation of the Serb bodies. And you just said to the Prosecutor that this was information which you had received from radio and television. Is that right, or did you see any such mutilation on any body yourself? And if so, could you tell us which.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: There were mutilated bodies, without arms and without heads and without legs, disemboweled, their guts spilled. I remember that. That is something that I remember seeing

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where did you see that, can you tell us, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: I saw that at Vis, when the attack was launched there, Setici, there were people who had been burnt, in Malesici too, and Rastosnica, as far as I can recollect just now. And also, there was in Kamenica at Glodjarsko Brdo, people without heads. And this was filmed on television, me taking a body and reuniting it -- taking a head and reuniting it with the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And help us with this: When did these events occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: These events -- I can't remember when they occurred. I don't remember the date or the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just roughly. Was it after the events in Zvornik that you first described when you were sent round collecting the bodies? Were these events after that or before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1775
utterances.text: After. It was afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Witness B-1775. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. Just wait a moment while the blinds are pulled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, I will give a short ruling in relation to the statement of Mr. Suad Zafic [phoen]. The Prosecution applied for provisional admission of this witness's statement under Rule 92 bis. It relates to the takeover of the Bratunac municipality, the witness's detention, and the subsequent execution of 29 men. The evidence to be given is cumulative as it deals with the takeover of the Bratunac municipality, about which evidence has been given. The statement is capable of admission under Rule 92 bis and admissible under that Rule, provided, of course, the various formalities are gone through. If they are gone through properly, then the statement can be admitted together with, it should be said, the witness being required to appear for cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is B-1455 -- I'm sorry, 1455 -- sorry, 1445. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are told 1455.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apology. It is 1455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that a binder of four exhibits be assigned a number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 454.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to begin your testimony before the Tribunal by taking a look at Prosecution Exhibit 454, tab 1. I want to draw your attention to the -- the name on the first line and ask you, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does the information contained in the right-hand column accurately reflect your professional and educational background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness move closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked if you would, Mr. Witness, to move closer to the microphone so that we can all hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that an exhibit number be assigned to the 92 bis package prepared for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 455, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber is in possession of your statement. I simply want to draw your attention to a particular portion of your statement and ask you some detailed questions about it. The portion of your statement I would like to draw your attention to is: Did there come a time when you, along with others, were detained in the Dom culture centre in Drinjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, I was detained in the cultural centre in Drinjaca on the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of how you and the other people there came to be collected and detained in that centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: On that same day, units of the reserve force of the JNA, together with local Serbs, came to our village and rounded up all the population they found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was the entire population that was present on that day placed in the Dom culture centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: All the population that was there on that day was driven to the cultural centre at Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 452, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the convenience of the Court, there was a separate copy of this placed in this binder and it's under tab 2, but perhaps we can withdraw it after this witness testifies. It was used with the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the building depicted in Prosecution Exhibit 452, tab 12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the cultural centre in Drinjaca, which I know very well. Behind it is the school that I attended for eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how many people altogether were gathered in this school?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And thank you to the usher. I'm finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand the question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many people altogether were gathered in the school at the time they were first detained in the school -- I'm sorry, in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: In the cultural centre, there were gathered 91 men, and I don't know the exact number of women and children. I think there were another 150 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when an army officer entered the cultural centre and addressed the people there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. An officer entered. He was a lieutenant by rank. His name was Branko Studen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you what he said, what was the ethnicity of the people that were gathered in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: All the people gathered in the cultural centre in Drinjaca were of Muslim faith and Bosniak nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This lieutenant, did he address the group? And if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: He did address the people. He addressed us. He first greeted us, and he said, "People, I know that you've done nothing wrong. I heard that from many people who are Serbs and who lived here together with you. You had good neighbourly relations. And I can guarantee that nothing will happen to you. Nevertheless, we will have to move you from your places of residence in Kostijerevo and Drinjaca, and you will probably be exchanged for Serbs living in Zenica, who, according to what he said, were having problems with the Muslim population over there, and that they will come to your houses, to your homes and inherit your property and you will go over there to inherit their homes and their property. I believe that that will be better for both peoples."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he make any statement about other people coming to the cultural centre to see the group there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. After this address - I can't say exactly how long it took, 15 to 20 minutes - he said, "I will go now and some men will come here to question you about certain military matters. These are people who specialise in military affairs. Don't be afraid. I've already told you that nothing will happen to you, no harm will befall you."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when the women and children were taken out of the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. Before he left, before he walked out, he ordered that the women and children have to leave the hall and that they would go in the direction of Tuzla, whereas we would follow them shortly, after being questioned by these military experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after Lieutenant Studen left, did there come a time when some other men did in fact come to the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the approximate period of time between the time Lieutenant Studen left and the arrival of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I think around 15 minutes went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the people who came to the -- the centre 15 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: When Branko Studen left, one of the soldiers who were guarding us and standing around us with their weapons pointed at us said that we should bend down our heads and put them between our knees as far as we were able. And we did that, and we waited. And 15 minutes later we heard behind our backs a strong banging on the door, and these people entered who were supposed to question us, but not to question us but they were carrying in their hands, as I saw well, metal sticks, wooden sticks. One of them even had a police truncheon. There were six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what you recall about what, if any, uniform they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They were armed with pistols hanging at the side, of the Skorpion brand. They had Rambo-type knives as we called them. They had black gloves with the fingers cut off, black caps rolled up. But this one who led them was not as tall as the rest. He wore a beard. He had dark glasses, and he had a hat on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based upon your experience, what you had prior to this date, did you draw a conclusion regarding what unit these men belonged to, based upon what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Based on the uniforms they wore, they looked most like members of Arkan's unit. But I cannot say that with certainty because I don't know whether they really were members of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after they arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: They ordered us to get up immediately, all of us, and then he said, "Let's hear some Chetnik songs." I had never sung Chetnik songs, nor am I familiar with them. I noticed among the people who were so afraid that they said, "Let's sing," but no one could start singing because people didn't know those songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Then he said, this man that I thought was in command because he was most provocative, this one who was shorter in height, wearing a camouflage uniform with a beard and glasses, "And now you're going to sing," he said. And people started to be taken out onto the stage and to be beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were they beaten with -- by hands, or were weapons used in the beating of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: They used what they were carrying in their hands, that is, metal bars and wooden sticks and this truncheon that I also saw, a police truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for what period of time did these beatings persist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: The beatings lasted right up until the evening, about 9.00 or 9.30. I didn't have a watch on, but I could notice through the windows that darkness had started falling, so it could have been around that time. Up until then, they continued beating the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the beatings were finished, did this group of men leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered us again to bend our heads as far down as we could, to our knees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when another group of men entered the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. Again, we were standing like that for a while, maybe 15 or 20 minutes with our heads bent down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were in the hall between the groups, would it have been possible for you and the other men there to have left the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was guarding -- or who was preventing you from leaving the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: A unit of the reserve force of the Yugoslav People's Army was always present, together with the local troops or members of that unit that were locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened after this other group arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: When this other group arrived, they ordered us to raise our heads and we looked at them. That was a unit that had never been there during the day. Nobody had noticed them. They were wearing uniforms that we knew were uniforms that used to be worn by the Chetniks during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction in connection with the transcript. I think it's a misunderstanding. I thought the witness said that it was a JNA unit that was there, was composed of reservists of the local population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there was a unit of the reserve force of the Yugoslav People's Army wearing uniforms, together with people who were also present who were attached to that unit and who were people who lived there in Drinjaca, who were attached to them. But there were very few from the area of Drinjaca, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Wait a minute. You can ask questions in due course, Mr. Milosevic. It looks at the moment that we're to adjourn, in fact. Witness B-1455, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. In this adjournment and any others there may be in the case, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. And that does include members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, inside the Drinjaca culture centre, without telling us their names or identifying -- or saying anything about them that would identify you, can you tell us what other members of your family were present at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. My father and three brothers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when these -- the second group of men who came in began to take out of the some detainees from the hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. When they entered, I noticed that they had on them these Chetnik uniforms. One could clearly see on their caps the so-called cockades. Some weren't wearing such hats. Some had some emblems that looked like eagles. And I also noticed that among them there were some that seemed to be rather tipsy. They were cracking jokes and kicking each other jokingly. And then we heard a voice say, "Down with your heads, you Turks, you balijas." They used all kind of derogatory terms in addressing us, and we bent down our heads. Then someone -- one of them was saying, "We need ten volunteers." I didn't dare apply. And no one did; no one volunteered. And then they said, "Why won't you volunteer? I have been a volunteer for so long and you don't want to be a volunteer. If you won't volunteer, I will choose." And we were listening to this. And then they counted up to ten; one, two, up to ten. "Do we have ten? Yes, we do." Then I heard chairs screeching, they were taking the men out. And then I heard, "Hurry out, you Turkish and Muslim motherfuckers." And I heard them hitting them and beating them, and one or two would scream out in pain. And they took them outside the hall. And then I heard them walking round the building, and they passed on our left side, and we heard bursts of fire coming from there. So I knew immediately that there were executions going on. Five minutes later or maybe ten minutes later - I can't be precise about that - they reentered the hall, and again they were looking for ten men. Again no one volunteered. And again, they counted up to ten, and once they had chosen the ten, they would take them round the building to the left of the cultural centre and I would hear bursts of fire at the same spot. This was repeated four times, until they came for the fifth time, and a soldier hit me with the -- with his gun and he said, "Get up. It's your turn." And when I got up, and they ordered me to go towards the exit, I saw that my father was waiting with me for the execution and some neighbours that I recognised very well. And then I saw another brother sitting in a row in front of me, and I noticed that already half the people in the hall were missing. And then in the same way they started hitting us with their rifle butts, cursing our Muslim and balija mothers, and calling us all other -- all kinds of names. And as we went out, there were two rows of soldiers. We had to pass between them. And the light was turned off, so you could see from the light coming from the hall, you could see the soldiers a little bit. But I didn't dare look at them. Then we went down the steps, as can be seen on this photograph, and then they ordered us to go to the left, in the same direction in which the other people had been taken. I saw them well. They all had -- there were many of them. They all had their rifles pointed at us. When we got close to the spot, one of the members of my group cried out, "Let's flee, men. They'll kill us all." They were close by, maybe 7 or 8 metres away. I think there were six or seven of them. And they had already received orders, "Shoot. What are you waiting for?" And they opened fire at us. I got a bullet in my left side here, and I fell on my stomach straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a few questions up until that point of the account. You've indicated -- or you've pointed to, when you were referring to where you were injured, you pointed to your left hip area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. I was hit here in the left hip. But fortunately, the bullet passed through the tissue. It didn't affect the bone. And I fell on my stomach. I could hear continued bursts of fire, people were falling. And when this was over, then they examined the people to see whether anyone may have survived. A soldier came up to me and kicked me in the behind, and he said, "I think this one is still alive." And the other one said, "Well, what are you waiting for? Fire a couple of more bullets at him." And then he fired a burst of fire in my back. So I got one bullet here in the right shoulder blade, and it came out here in the front. It was an entry and exit wound. The pain was so strong that I only just managed to remain conscious. And I felt as if I was falling down a precipice. I had black lights before my eyes. But I remained conscious and I could hear them talking as the blood streamed down my body. They started crying out at one another. They started screaming, shooting into the air. And then one said, "What are we going to do? We don't have any more ammunition." And the other one said, "What do you mean? There's several more boxes in the centre down there." And then they left. I heard him pass by me. When I was quite certain that there was no one left next to me, I tried to get up, but this arm was completely out of action, so I slowly got up on my feet, holding my arm, and then in a couple of seconds I saw many men around me, lying dead. I ran by the school that was nearby, but in the school playground, which was perhaps some 20 metres away from the cultural centre, there's just a fence separating them. As I ran by the school, I saw another group of people lying dead. They were dead. And one man was still crying out in pain. He was probably so badly wounded that he still hadn't passed away. He was crying out for help, but I just ran on to save my own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just -- you've indicated, and you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you were referring to your arm, you were indicating with your hand your right arm. Is it your right arm that you felt -- or you couldn't feel as you were lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: My right one. Yes, my right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've also indicated your injury. Just so that the record reflects what you pointed to, you pointed to your back -- your back near the right shoulder as the entry wound and you pointed to the front part of your right shoulder as the exit wound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I need to hear your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I continued running in the direction of my village, Kostijerevo. I ran across some meadows. And there's an Orthodox cemetery there that I am familiar with, very well-acquainted with. And then there's the woods that start there, about 500 metres from the Dom, the cultural centre, which remained behind me. I couldn't run any further because I was exhausted and my wounds were hurting me a great deal. While I was running upwards, I heard the gunshots being fired down by the Dom. When I entered the woods or forest, I laid down a little bit because I realised that I was losing consciousness, and I held onto the shrubs to avoid losing consciousness. And I wanted to see what my wound looked like, so I took a finger and placed my entire index finger into the hollow of the wound, and it went straight through. I thought everything was hollow, but it wasn't. I pulled out my finger, and the wound was enormous. And then I placed all my clothing across the wound and held it in place like this. Through the branches of the trees, I was able to distinguish some streetlights by the Dom, the centre. I wasn't able to see the soldiers, but I did hear on three or four -- three or four intervals, five or ten minutes away from each other, these bursts of gunfire. And then I realised and was quite certain that all the people that I had seen and what I had experienced, that they had in fact all been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, from that vantage point, were you able to see a truck arrive at the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: While I was sitting there and having a rest, some 20 minutes later, after the shooting had stopped, a struck switched on its engines, its motor, 100 metres from the centre, and it reached the spot where the actual shooting had taken place. You could hear the truck doors being opened, because it made a noise, and then I heard the voice of a man. I think it was a Serb. I would say he was a Serb probably from the village of Drinjaca. And when he saw all these people, he shouted out, "People, what have you done? What's all this? What have you done?" And he repeated this several times over, until they quietened him. Something was going on. I couldn't see exactly what was happening, because it was too far away and it was night-time as well. Now, the truck doors closed again. I saw them -- I heard them being closed, rather, the sides -- the side doors of the truck some half an hour later, and the truck went back to the shop, which is about 100 metres away Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the centre, the cultural centre, and the engines were switched off again, the motor was switched off again. And then I continued moving towards my village, but I didn't dare enter the village itself. I went around the outskirts. And after I had gone 100 to 150 metres to the next forest across a meadow, I happened to see some lights which were moving around the village, being flashed round the village, and suddenly the houses were alight and I heard some people talking further down, people who had -- who were setting fire to the houses, but I didn't dare move. All I could do was watch the houses burning. Once they had finished setting fire to the houses, they continued along the path that I had crossed, or road I had crossed, across the meadow, and they went on further towards the houses in my village. But the houses that were closest by, let's say some 300 metres away, they didn't set fire to those houses. I assumed that they knew - and I know those houses very well - people -- they belonged to people who worked abroad and they were well-to-do people, so I assumed they wanted to loot the houses first. That's why they spared them, didn't set fire to them straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention back to the cultural centre. Did your father and brothers survive what occurred in the cultural centre that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, they did not survive the shooting. They were executed that evening. And in 1998 their bodies were exhumed in the village of Glumina, and the location was called Ramin Grob. All the victims were pulled out - there were some others from the village - and then they appealed to us via the media from the villages of Drinjaca -- or rather, the municipality of Drinjaca and some other villages, because when they found some documents, they were able to establish that they were people who were not natives of Drinjaca or the surrounding villages -- who were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who were natives of Drinjaca and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we were invited to come to Tuzla to a commemorative centre there to identify the bodies that were laid out there. There were a lot of people present during this identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we get to that, if I can just ask you a few questions. Are you aware of anybody other than you that survived from -- what happened in the cultural centre that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes; two other men survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask you not to mention their names. Did there come a time when you made a list of all the people that you could recall were present that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. I did make a list of the people whom I was with in the cultural centre. And those lists have been sent on to various places, to the state media, the local media, The Hague Tribunal, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 454, tab 3. And my question to you is: Is this one of the lists that you yourself made of the victims of what happened in Drinjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, these are the lists of people. And I compiled the lists myself personally. On the list are all the people who were detained that particular day, except for the five people I mention who were shot in the village, who tried to resist the arrest, and they were shot on the spot, executed on the spot. Their bodies were later found and buried as deemed fit. I didn't see the shooting of those people myself, but they put up a resistance, according to what others said, having been in the woods round about and saw the shooting going on, so that there is clear-cut evidence that they were in fact shot by this army and later on they were buried in a dignified manner. That's as far as those five individuals go. As to all the others on the list, they were all people who were incarcerated in Drinjaca with me, and I'm quite sure that those people were shot, they were executed. We have the documents from the Ministry of the Interior, the Tuzla canton, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the commission for collecting facts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll just point out to the Chamber that the English translation of that exhibit does not repeat the names contained in the original. So in order to properly use the English translation, one must refer to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you took a look at -- well, let me, before I do that -- I'm sorry. Did you actually go to Glumina, the site where the bodies were exhumed from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: No, I did not go to Glumina, where the bodies were uncovered, because I never again went back to my native village or my native municipality for the fear that you can well imagine that I feel. But I did attend the identification process in Tuzla at the centre there. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to unnecessarily ask you to deal with difficult matters, so if I could ask you to simply say: When you saw some of the bodies exhumed from Glumina, were you able to positively identify some members of your family? Just yes or no would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And which members of your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I identified both my father and my three brothers. However, my father and one of my brothers, I found it very easy to identify because they were wearing -- they were in black plastic bags with zips on them, and those bodies were very well preserved. And it looked as if they had just been shot several months ago. Whereas, the other bodies were more difficult to identify. We had to identify them on the basis of the clothing they were wearing because all that remained were the bones. But as I know full well what my other two brothers were wearing on that particular day, I found them there. With the help of the commission, we were able to establish that those people, after the expert analyses were taken and the bone marrow extracted, they indeed certified that they were members of my family. And this is -- they are now in a civilised manner buried, which is a thing that I'm grateful for. And their graves exist, they've been marked, and you can read the names of the people who were buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, when were you asked to go and make these identifications? Can you simply tell us the month and year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: That was -- I don't know the exact date, but it was in the month of October 1998. I think that's when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a list of names of identified bodies from Glumina. I'm going to ask you: Do you recognise, without necessarily calling out the name, but do you recognise some of the people listed in that list of bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the number of this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies. 454, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I apologise but could you just tell me what I'm to do with these lists. How am I to say that I recognise them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you -- is the name of your father and brothers on that list? Without telling us the number next to their name, just simply if you could tell us whether you saw their names on the list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Here I have the name of my father, and here I have the name of my youngest brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to those two names, do you recognise other names of people who were present in Drinjaca, Dom Kulture, on the night you've described for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes. Here on this first list, under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it's not necessary to go through and actually identify them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I recognise many people here from my village, as well as from Drinjaca, Sopotnik, and Dzevanje. Those are the names of the villages. Because it all belongs to one municipality, all these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my final question to you here today is: Could you, in a sentence or two, describe what permanent effects you have suffered as a result of what happened in Drinjaca on the night that you've described for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I have lasting effects in my right shoulder from the entrance/exit wound. I had bone fractures here. And from the wounding, I remain a permanent invalid. The doctors have done everything in their power for me to regain the normal movements of my arm, like the left one, but as the wound was a complicated one and the muscles had been severed, they would have to do implants, transplanting muscles from other parts of my body to this area here. After thinking long and hard about this, they decided to leave things as they were, so I'll have to live like this for the rest of my life. As to the wound that passed through my left thigh -- hip, luckily the bullet did not fracture my bones, but I do feel pain when the weather changes. And if I were to sleep on that side, then I feel pain too. And of course, after the shooting, after I was shot, I had nightmares for many years afterwards and my body shook. I experienced great nervousness. So I decided to carry on and continue with my treatment. As for psychological treatment, I have improved a great deal in that respect and I am very grateful to the doctors for taking care of me. But unfortunately, my right hand will not be able to move around as it previously did. I cannot conduct any rotation with my arm, I can just move it up and down. So I have to use my left hand to eat with. It was difficult for me to get used to using my left hand more but I have succeeded, and I can still write with my right hand. But I'll never be able to perform the job I did beforehand. I have to do some menial tasks today, which are very poorly paid. But the important thing, of course, is that I am alive and that my mother, who lost three of her sons and her husband, has me and can look at me alive in the state I'm in now and she's happy to see me alive and I'm happy to see my own family, my children, my mother, and my friends. So much from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got an exhibit number for the statement, Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was 455, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1455, I shall do my best not to ask you questions which might upset you in any way, in view of the fact that you have lost members of your family, but I would like us to clarify some points. Let me ask a preliminary question: From all the descriptions you've given us in -- on different occasions, the statements you have made - I'm looking at your statements now - and I have also been listening to what you said during this short examination-in-chief, is it clear that there was no JNA unit which participated in all those events, nor was in the area at all at the time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: It was clear to us that a reserve unit of the Yugoslav People's Army was present there. And we know, Mr. Milosevic, that in the former Yugoslav People's Army the young men ranged from the ages of 19, 20, and so on, they were in the regular army. But -- so they were there between the ages of 20, and 30 was the highest age. So they wore uniforms that did not associate us with the Chetnik uniforms, but they wore uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think anything else is switched on for this interference to be caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The whole reserve complement of a local character throughout Yugoslavia, the Territorial Defence, they all had the same uniforms, just like the JNA. There wasn't any difference. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: It is right that the reserve units of the JNA didn't have different uniforms; that is to say, their uniforms were no different than the regular JNA army, Mr. Milosevic, the reserve force from the regular Yugoslav army. So they had the same uniforms. I just regret that the Court has so little time for us to be more specific. But when I tell you that when the weapons were confiscated from the inhabitants of Drinjaca, Sopotnik, and the other place, there were people with the same uniforms with the Yugoslav flag placed on the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the disarmament process, disarming the people, I assume you will remember that the army had the task of disarming both sides, and especially to disarm the paramilitary formations. By confiscating the weapons was one operation, but I'm talking about the events you testified about. And as far as I was able to gather, from what you said here orally during your testimony and from what you wrote in your statement, all the people that you enumerate did not have any JNA insignia but various other insignia that could not have belonged to the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Sir, I said that the persons who were wearing uniforms, uniforms of the reservist formation of Yugoslavia, were there when the population was rallied up and when they stood guard over them in Drinjaca, in the cultural centre. It was only later that the paramilitaries turned up wearing different uniforms, the Chetnik uniforms and others, those who beat up the people and ultimately shot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when you say, for example, referring to the six men who were -- the six men who beat up the people in the hall, and you say they had Skorpions, knives, et cetera, and that this commander of theirs had a beard, these were all things that you stated, are they not? You know that the JNA didn't allow anybody to wear beards and that the JNA members had to be well turned out and that the issued weapons did not include Skorpions in the JNA. What was used was exclusively domestically produced weapons by the Crnovo Zastavo or Red Star company. They were the manufacturers of the regular issued weapons. I assume you know that, in view of the fact that you did your regular military service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I understand what you are saying. But you must understand me too. That particular unit of the reservists really did not -- of the JNA really didn't have beards and they didn't have Skorpions and they didn't have knives in their hands. They had weapons that were manufactured in Yugoslavia and the uniforms you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, to link all this up. What date are you referring to? Although, it says here. But what date, what period of time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I'm talking about the date which was the 30th of May, 1992. This event took place on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that already on the 30th of May the JNA had withdrawn from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina by that date? Do you know when the Army of the Republika Srpska was established and when those reservists that you talk about ceased to be a component part of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and when all these changes took place? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have not come here to speak about when the Serbian army within Bosnia-Herzegovina was established and when the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sure the competent authorities have all those facts and figures. They know about it better than me. But it was a coincidence that they withdrew on the 30th of May, that the JNA withdrew from the territory precisely on that date. It ceased to exist as of that date and then the Serbian army began to be formed, I assume. I know nothing about those dates. All I'm testifying about are things that I saw myself. What I'm not sure about and the things I don't know about, I don't want to talk about because I don't know about those other facts and dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully respect that. But I just wanted us to clarify that it couldn't have been the JNA or any units of the regular army at all. And the fact that this went on in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a tragedy, of course, for all three ethnic groups, for all three nations. There's no challenging that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You shouldn't have a general discussion of these matters. Now, what specific questions have you for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have specific questions, Mr. May, with respect to the witness's testimony and statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, on page 2, you say that the first free elections took place in 1991, and that people did not trust each other because they feared that the national parties, who represented the interests of other ethnic groups, could win the elections and take power to the detriment, to the disadvantage of the other side. That's what you say in your statement, roughly, and that was the atmosphere that prevailed at the time in those parts. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is true that there was a technical problem that arose with respect to the date of the first re-elections to be held in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And later on I asked the Tribunal to change the date. It was in 1990, in fact. In my statement, this wasn't the essential point for me, whether they were held in 1990 or 1991, these elections. But it is true that they were in October in 1990, as far as I heard from people, and it is also true and correct that when the people went to vote in the free elections, the national parties were there in the elections. So there was a lack of trust. But this did not manifest itself as strongly until the referendum that took place in March 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the Bosniaks and the Croats went to the polls and voted to their century-old homeland, whereas the Serbs did not want to go to the polls. They told us, "You go and vote, but we're going to stay in Yugoslavia, because Yugoslavia is our country."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just make this clear, Mr. 1455: It wasn't my intention to see any differences in the times, whether you were talking about 1990 or 1991, the date. What I was interested in was an explanation of the atmosphere and mood that prevailed during the elections, independently of the fact of whether it was in 1990 or 1991. It was just this atmosphere of distrust on the part of the ethnic nationalist parties and the fear that if one national party were to win the elections, they would work to the disadvantage of the other ethnic group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that people thought that way. But we learnt -- we knew very well who attacked whom later on and who it was that perpetrated the genocide, if we look at those ruling parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, who knows this and whether it is common knowledge, we'll discuss that in due course. But you say that you noticed that people who had been friends previously ceased to be friends any more. And you say that in paragraph 2, page 2, that they were singing nationalistic songs at wedding ceremonies that the other side found derogatory. And so I wanted to ask you -- insulting. I wanted to ask you some indirect questions. I'm not setting any traps for you. I just want to ask you quite simply what led up to all this -- or rather, I'm asking you this: Is it true that the leadership, led by Alija Izetbegovic, for instance, quite clearly stated loud and clear what their ambitions were with respect to creating an Islamic state under the dominance of the Muslims? Did they state that publicly loud and clear? And anyway, if you remember, he publicly stated that he would sacrifice peace for a Muslim Bosnia. Do you remember that? Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: That question isn't really related to my testimony very much, but of course what I can say is this: We did not want a war, because we knew that if we were to start it, first of all, and we didn't have anything to start it with, then we knew we would be the first to be attacked. And what you say about Izetbegovic, remember what Karadzic said in Sarajevo, who said, "If war does come about, that is to say, if the Muslims and Croats decide for a sovereign Bosnia, then one of the ethnic groups would disappear, that is to say, the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you'd have to ask him that, not me. But even that position was a position against war, an anti-war position. The Serbs were, of course, against a war. But you said a moment ago that tensions had increased when the referendum was held and when the decision taken by the Muslims and Croats was to have an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're a young man, but you certainly know full well that Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of three nations; Serbs, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This kind of general debate has nothing to do with the witness. We can hear all about it in due course, if it's relevant, but concentrate on what the witness has come here to give evidence about, which is what happened, particularly in the cultural centre. You can ask him questions about that, rather than a general political debate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I believe I am entitled to ask questions in connection with what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
