utterances.text: No. You can ask questions on his evidence or indeed what's in his statement. Now, have you any questions on those particular topics?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you heard the witness saying that tensions increased after the referendum, and that is what I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was all to do with your suggestions and your questions. Now, what -- if you've got a passage in his statement you want to ask him about, you can do so. But he gave no evidence here about those tensions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, a moment ago on his own, without me asking him anything, he said that relations soured, especially after the referendum. Please check the transcript. After the referendum at which the decision was taken for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're helped by this. Much time is wasted with every witness as to what happened, the referendum, and all the rest of it, these political matters. We've heard it all before. Now, you can ask this witness specific questions. Now, would you like to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask him the questions that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. feel I need to ask him. It is not up to me to assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But rather, to convey the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it doesn't assist us, then you're not going to be allowed to ask the questions, because they're not relevant. Now, let's get on with it, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this tension which was present throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina culminated with the killing of a Serb, Nikola Gardovic, and the wounding of Milenko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over all this. We've been over all this. This casting of blame is of no assistance at all. Now, he's dealing with very specific events; murder of a great number of people in that cultural centre. If you challenge that, you should do so, rather than this constant harking back to events much before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you are bringing witnesses here from another state to testify about very specific matters about which I certainly cannot know except from information collected by my associates. Therefore, it is quite inopportune for us to debate here whether a killing occurred or not. I am trying to clarify things, taking into consideration the witness's statement and his testimony here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 2, paragraph 9 of your statement that towards the end of 1991 Serbs started organising village guards in order to protect themselves from Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, after the end of the war in Croatia, we held joint guard duty with the Serbs, together, with hunting weapons that we had on both sides. We held those guards to prevent infiltration by someone who might cause unrest. Amongst us, who had such good relations, they were exemplary and few like it in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, when the question in connection with the referendum arose for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs simply said, "We can't go on like this any more. You will have to take your side and defend yourself and we will defend ourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for explaining that in that way, because this is what it says in this paragraph: "Towards the end of 1991 --" this is paragraph 2 on page 2 -- or rather, page 1, really, of your statement. So: "Towards the end of 1991, Serbs started organising village guards in order to protect themselves from Muslims." So my question is: So the Serbs were in danger, since they organised village guards to protect themselves from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that was their opinion, that they were protecting themselves from the Muslims, because there was no third nation there. Who would they defend themselves from, the Finns? They were afraid of us. But we gave them assurances that we could never hurt them, that there was no need for them to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to witness to have his own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can read the next sentence too. Wait a minute. Let him find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is on page 2 of your statement. In the Serbian language, it is the second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's paragraph number 9, handwritten number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Witness B-1455, do you see that sentence that you've been asked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I see that sentence. And I answered that question for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you just perhaps read out the next two sentences. Do you see those sentences: "We Muslims offered them to do the joint guards, but they refused. They said Muslims and Serbs do not have anything in common any more." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that. And of course, when they decided to have independent guards, what else could we do but organise ourselves to protect our homes and our village using what we had legally, like hunting weapons. Some people managed to purchase some weapons on the black market, but they were very few, people who had a lot of money. One had to have 1.500 German marks for such a rifle. So it was normal for us to protect our homes and our village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue right where, Mr. May, you stopped in quoting the sentence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It continues to say: "Because we Muslims voted for a sovereign and independent Bosnia. The Serbs wanted to stay in Yugoslavia." Now, tell me, please, was it normal for them to remain in Yugoslavia and do you consider them, too, being an equal nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, having the right to express their will as to staying in Yugoslavia or leaving it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what his views are about that. That's what he said happened. Whether it was right or wrong and what the rights and wrongs of it all were do not matter as far as this witness is concerned. He's just describing what happened in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to say that, "You Muslims decided to arm yourselves, that the president of the Crisis Staff, Mehmed Hodzic, formed guards in the villages of Kostijerevo and Drinjaca." You say, "The plan was to protect our houses." Now, tell me, who were you protecting your houses from when you said a moment ago that the Serbs were in danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: I didn't say that the Serbs were in danger. They said, "Now, if you vote for an independent and sovereign Bosnia, we are going to remain in Yugoslavia. We have nothing in common with you. We will keep a guard duty round our houses and you do that over there, so we have nothing in common any more." And of course we had a man who represented our Crisis Staff to preserve the population, and what legal weapons we had the Serbs knew about it. They also had legal weapons. Because our area is a hunting area. So we guarded our houses separately. But there was no incident. Never was there any incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in mid-March 1992 the Serbs established their own police station and the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik. Both were based in Karakaj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't hold Zvornik. If they had held Zvornik, they wouldn't have been based in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Zvornik was a town with a majority Muslim population. And Karakaj had a majority Serb population. It was an industrial zone, quite a large settlement with a majority Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they formed the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik in a Serbian settlement and not a Muslim one, and Zvornik had a majority Muslim population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is true that that is how it was. But why, then, did they cross over into our territory, torch our houses, and kill our people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what we are talking about. Why did the Serbs organise themselves in Karakaj? You speak about that in paragraph 2, page 3. Was it because they were expelled from Zvornik? In your statement you say that Muslims, because they were in the majority, stayed in Zvornik. What happened to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: The Serbs stayed in Zvornik too, just as did the Muslims in Karakaj. At the point in time when those municipalities were being formed, nobody had hurt anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before there were any moves taken by the Serbs there was a mobilisation of Muslim forces and the formation of units in Zvornik? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: When the municipality was divided up and a little quantity -- a small quantity of weapons were distributed to both sides by the Ministry of the Interior, they were M-48 rifles, and when they had formed their own municipality and Ministry of the Interior in Karakaj, a unit was formed of Territorial Defence to protect their homes, villages, and the town, and it moved out to Kula Grad. I said that there was very heavy fighting over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say M-48 rifles. This is a simple non-automatic rifle. All the others are automatic or semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I saw three such rifles being issued to three men in our village, M-48 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just linking this to the part of your testimony when a Serb told you to go in front of him and started shooting at you and then you say he had to cock his rifle each time, and this saved you because it gave you a chance to escape. Is that right? So that Serb, who was leading you, also had this trophy rifle which was not part of the standard JNA weaponry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is true that he accompanied me holding an M-48 rifle. However, when I was in Mjedovo Brdo - this is neighbouring village to mine - I found all the neighbours from my village there and most of them had automatic rifles, light machine-guns, semi-automatic rifles, and I saw him holding this particular rifle and he escorted me with that rifle. And that may have been lucky for me, because if he had had an automatic rifle, I may not have been here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I'm just saying that, using your own example, you showed that they were armed with the same trophy weapons that you say you had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just saw that rifle on him. As for all the other neighbours, they had automatic, semi-automatic rifles, and light machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the first paragraph on page 3, you say, "Since the Muslims were in the majority, they stayed in Zvornik." Before that, you say that the Serbs had formed a municipality in Karakaj. "We the Muslims realised that we should prepare ourselves for war. People were worried. Some started packing their belongings and leaving their homes to go to Tuzla." That is what you say, that the majority population remained in Zvornik and realised that they should prepare for war. Isn't, then, what you stated here the reason for the tensions, including for the arming of the Serbs, that is, that the reason was that the preparation -- the preparations that you the Muslims, the majority population in Zvornik, started preparing for war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you have any signs of oncoming war, we had to use all available means should we be attacked. And there were indications to that effect and it was only normal for us to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say that there were indications that they would attack you, is it true and well-known that precisely in those days, that is, March and the beginning of April 1992, prior to the conflict in Zvornik, attacks had started on Serb villages in your area, precisely by Muslim extremists and paramilitary formations? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must give me the names of those villages for me to perhaps be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me look for that, for those names. For instance, do you know that prior to the conflict in Zvornik, in the village of Sapna, an ambush was set for a column -- or rather, a vehicle of the reserve force of the JNA that was withdrawing and that warrant officer Mika Stanojovic [phoen] was killed on that occasion, as well as several other people being seriously wounded? Do you remember that incident when the people that you say were preparing to defend themselves had organised an ambush prior to any attacks and actually attack members of the reserve force killed this warrant officer and wounded several people? This was in Sapna on the 5th of April, 1992. Is that right or not, Mr. 1455?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I hear this for the first time from you, and I really don't remember any of it. This is something that I learn of for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you never heard about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Believe me, I never of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do believe you. And do you remember that as early as mid-March 1992 there were arrests of a group of Serb youths in Carmani in Donji Kamenica who were mistreated by Avdija Omerovic -- he organised it and he works in the police. This is an incident that seriously increased tensions in the Zvornik area. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I hear that for the first time too, and I am unable to comment on it because I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I fully appreciate that. Just say you don't know, and we can move on. Is it true that in that area, just around that time, a paramilitary formation was organised known as the Patriotic League of Nations, as it called itself? Actually, it was a paramilitary formation of Muslim extremists, the Patriotic League of Nations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I do know that the first unit that I know was at Kula Grad near Zvornik consisted of a certain number of men who had left the town and who were defending themselves at Kula Grad. But I know -- don't know of that name. I have heard of the Patriotic League, but that it was there -- such a unit was there and that's what it was called, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the code name of this man, Captain Almir? In fact, Samir Misovic, who organised the Patriotic League in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of a man by that name called Almir, but I never knew his real first and last name. And that he organised the defence of Zvornik and Kula Grad from attacks by the JNA and Serbian paramilitary units who, 20 days later, took control of Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that those formations of Muslim forces had held Zvornik, if the Serbs took over control later on. How can they take it over if they hadn't held it before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there was no resistance in the town of Zvornik because there were both Serbs and Muslims living there, and those people, even if they did organise defence of the town, as they did, they were located at Kula Grad. And as far as I know, the battles -- all the battles were waged there, though I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that on the day that the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, on the 6th of April, that in Sarajevo and in other locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were armed conflicts involving the death of 14 people and the injury of more than 100, before the conflicts in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1455
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I saw on television that there were some incidents in Sarajevo. But could you tell me what happened on the 4th of April, before the attack on Zvornik, what had happened in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I could answer that question for you, but I assume they wouldn't let me do it. But I'll tell you. When the Green Berets captured Bijeljina and blocked with roadblocks the centre of Bijeljina and when a witness, Alija Gusalic, who even witnessed here, went to throw a hand grenade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is going to rehearse some of the evidence. We're going to adjourn now. There's a matter which the Prosecution want to raise, so we won't adjourn precisely -- May we take it that this witness will be back on Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe that is not a difficulty for the witness. I haven't personally checked. Perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: B-1455, can you be back, please, on Monday morning to conclude your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you wouldn't mind waiting now. We're just going to deal with one or two administrative matters, nothing to do with your evidence. Except for this: We will then conclude this witness's evidence before we do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very short matter I want to raise: The Chamber knows that we've been providing to the Chamber and to the accused and the amici documents from time to time. One is called a fullbox document and one, I think, called a chronology. They have been prepared on a particular computer system. There is a possibility of our converting those documents to a new or different computer system that offers considerable advantages for those conducting trials. And this is -- I'm saying this in court so that the accused can listen, because I think it's really with him in mind that I'm saying it. The new system offers particular advantages to those preparing and handling complex trials of this nature. The new system is one with which I know that your legal officers are, to a degree, or have to a degree become acquainted. It seemed to me sensible that before we make the decision, if we do, to convert what is a very usable tool already, to a tool that will come in a different format, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we should discuss that with the interested parties, including the amici, the accused's associates, if they are prepared to be involved, and your legal officers. So I'm attempting to fix a meeting, probably on Monday, because we want to move reasonably swiftly with this if we are going to change the format in which we present documents to you -- attempt to arrange a meeting where all the parties will be invited to attend. If the accused feels he cannot send his associates, then we will, I hope, have the meeting without a representation by his associates, although that would be unfortunate. What I will then do is have a minute prepared of the meeting and I will provide them with that minute in due course. The preferred course would, of course, be for his associates to attend, because the reality is that the resolution of this case will be assisted by the best - and this may well be the most modern - systems for handling the material that's being produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't a system which was -- there was some talk of introducing a system sometime ago. I can't remember what it was -- which didn't find favour. This is a new system altogether; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know the system of which Your Honour is referring. I do know that the system to which I'm referring is one that your officers Ms. Featherstone and Mr. Boas have been introduced, and my understanding is that they viewed it favourably. Whether they did that on their own account or on Your Honours' accounts, I'm not sure, but it's something we would like to discuss with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I guess we'll have to see how the system that you have in mind works. And in particular, of course, it must not be a system that adds to the -- to the -- to what is already a very difficult trial to manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have that very much in mind. I also have in mind that the present documentation, which is particularly suitable for those who prefer not to use computers, is a very usable series of tools. I'm concerned, amongst other things, that any new system would enable us to replicate or continue providing documentation in that form so that it would serve both those who prefer not to use computers or who don't have access to them at the particular time and those who find computer systems more useful. But it's because of the different audiences to which these documents are going - by which I mean Your Honours, the accused, his associates, and the amici - that I'm anxious that we not take a step that would be substantial in resource implications for us unless we can be sure that it's going to be a sensible step to take for all audiences concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the point must be that the Trial Chamber retains the right to pass on the usability of any system that is going to affect the rights of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we've finished that topic, if Mr. Groome would help us about Monday, and also the accused, so he can know who we're going to hear from next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, after this witness is B-1098, a witness that I don't expect -- I expect will take us to the end of Monday, but we may finish him even before the end of Monday. The witness after him is C-047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, can you provide an updated list today, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm informed that that's already been provided, Your Honour, and I assume it will be distributed shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're working out, Mr. Milosevic, how long you've got. You've got about 50 minutes on Monday morning, which will give you an hour and a half with this witness. And you should be getting a list of the other witnesses. We'll make sure that that happens, so you know what to prepare for next week. We'll adjourn now until Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
